headline: Giant telescope in Chile turns for the first time

sources.title: Extremely Large Telescope reaches a major milestone | Space photo of the day for July 13, 2026
Rotating the Extremely Large Telescope (video, European Southern Observatory (ESO))

chunks.text: Engineers in Chile's Atacama Desert have {{pulled off}} something [[amazing]]. At the construction site of the Extremely Large Telescope, or ELT, they turned the giant [[telescope]] [[structure]] around its [[axis]] for the very first time. To get it moving, a small team first pushed the machine [[by hand]], just centimeters [[at a time]], while others {{looked on}}. After that, powerful [[motors]] {{took over}} and completed a full turn.

verbs.wrong: To work together well as one team
verbs.correct: To succeed in doing something difficult
verbs.why: A small team can pull off a surprise party in one afternoon, and a chef can pull off a huge dinner without help. Engineers in Chile pulled off the first full turn of the giant telescope structure.

verbs.wrong: To supervise something in order to keep it safe
verbs.correct: To watch something as an observer only
verbs.why: People look on as workers lift a heavy beam, and neighbors look on when something exciting happens nearby. Other workers looked on as a small team pushed the huge telescope by hand.

verbs.wrong: To make a loud humming noise all day
verbs.correct: To take control of something from someone else
verbs.why: A relief driver can take over during a long road trip, and an assistant coach might take over practice when the coach is sick. Here powerful motors took over once workers had pushed the structure a little by hand.

chunks.text: The ELT is a huge machine, but it moves in a very gentle way. The whole structure is {{held up}} by a [[layer]] of oil only 80 microns thin, which lets it [[slide]] almost without any [[effort]]. When it is done, the telescope's main mirror will be {{made up of}} 798 [[segments]] of special glass. Together, they will {{carry out}} the work of one giant mirror, 39 meters [[wide]].

verbs.wrong: To delay something or make it late
verbs.correct: To support the weight of something
verbs.why: Thick wooden beams hold up an old barn roof, and a steel frame can hold up a heavy bridge. A layer of oil only 80 microns thin holds up the entire telescope structure, letting it turn with almost no effort.

verbs.wrong: To be cleaned very carefully before use
verbs.correct: To form the whole of something from smaller parts
verbs.why: A soccer team is made up of eleven players, and a good salad is made up of fresh vegetables and a light dressing. The telescope's main mirror will be made up of 798 separate pieces of special glass.

verbs.correct: To do or perform a task
verbs.why: Doctors carry out tests before a surgery, and a company can carry out a plan step by step. Together, the 798 mirror segments will carry out the work of one giant mirror 39 meters wide.

chunks.text: The numbers behind the project are [[hard to imagine]]. [[Right now]], the metal parts {{add up to}} about 3,500 metric tons. That weight will {{go up}} to more than 4,600 metric tons [[once]] the mirrors and science [[instruments]] are [[in place]]. Because the whole thing can turn, the telescope will be able to point at any area of the sky and study [[faraway]] [[galaxies]].

verbs.wrong: To seem sensible or make sense
verbs.correct: To reach a certain total when combined
verbs.why: Grocery items can add up to sixty dollars fast, and small savings add up to a large sum over the years. Right now the telescope's metal parts already add up to about 3,500 metric tons.

verbs.wrong: To rise above and pass a fixed limit
verbs.correct: To rise or become higher in amount
verbs.why: Gas prices can go up sharply during the summer, and a fever can go up quickly overnight. The telescope's total weight will go up to more than 4,600 metric tons once the mirrors are in place.

chunks.text: This test was an important [[milestone]] [[on the road to]] finishing the ELT. Builders [[expect to]] {{wrap up}} the work around 2028. When it opens, the telescope's [[enormous]] mirror will make it {{stand out}} as the largest optical telescope in the world. Many [[astronomers]] already {{look forward to}} the first clear images it will [[capture]].

verbs.wrong: To hand a job to another team
verbs.why: A team might wrap up a long meeting before lunch, and a crew can wrap up filming after months of work. Builders expect to wrap up this massive telescope project around the year 2028.

verbs.wrong: To keep working well for many years without failing
verbs.correct: To be clearly better or more noticeable than others
verbs.why: A bright red coat can stand out in a crowd, and a strong essay can stand out among hundreds of others. When finished, this telescope will stand out as the largest optical telescope in the world.

verbs.wrong: To carefully plan and prepare for a future event
verbs.correct: To feel happy and excited about a future event
verbs.why: Kids look forward to summer vacation for months, and fans look forward to a favorite band's next album. Astronomers already look forward to the first clear images this giant telescope will capture.

mainIdea.s: Engineers in Chile pulled off the first full turn of a giant new telescope structure this year. Workers moved it by hand at first, and then powerful motors took over to finish the whole turn.
mainIdea.why: The story says engineers pulled off the first full rotation, with workers pushing by hand before motors took over to complete it.

mainIdea.s: The successful test turn means the huge telescope in Chile has already begun to capture images of faraway galaxies. Its mirror now sits fully in place, so astronomers can start their research work.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the telescope cannot capture images yet. The article says the mirror segments and instruments go in later, with the whole project set to wrap up around 2028.

mainIdea.s: A separate group of researchers working in Chile's Atacama Desert recently shared new findings about a distant black hole. Their work used an older telescope, not the giant new structure built nearby.
mainIdea.why: This is about a black hole study from a different telescope. The article is about the first turn of the new Extremely Large Telescope structure.

tf.s: Motors moved the whole telescope first, and then workers took over by hand.
tf.why: It was the other way around. Workers pushed it by hand first, and then the motors took over to finish the turn.

tf.s: The telescope's main mirror will be made up of 798 segments of special glass.
tf.why: The story says the main mirror will be made up of 798 glass segments.

tf.s: Engineers pulled off the first full rotation of the giant structure.
tf.why: The engineers pulled off the difficult job of turning the huge structure for the first time.

tf.s: The team decided to wrap up the whole telescope by 2026.
tf.why: Builders expect to wrap up the work around 2028, not 2026.

tf.s: The heavy structure is held up by a very thin layer of oil.
tf.why: The story says the structure is held up by a layer of oil only 80 microns thin.

tf.s: The telescope's main mirror will be made up of a single giant piece of glass.
tf.why: False. The mirror will be made up of 798 separate segments of special glass.

lines.text: Engineers in Chile just {{pulled off}} a beautiful test. The world's biggest telescope turned for the first time.
The one in the Atacama Desert?
That's it, the Extremely Large Telescope. A small team pushed the structure by hand, centimeters at a time, while the others {{looked on}}. Then the motors {{took over}} and completed a full turn.
They moved a giant telescope by hand? [[How is that possible]]?
The whole thing is {{held up}} by a layer of oil only 80 microns thin, so it slides almost without effort.
[[That's genius]]. How big is it exactly?
The metal parts {{add up to}} about 3,500 tons now, and the weight will {{go up}} past 4,600 once the mirrors are installed.
The main mirror will be {{made up of}} 798 glass segments that {{carry out}} the work of one giant mirror, 39 meters wide.
When can astronomers actually use it?
Builders hope to {{wrap up}} around 2028. It will {{stand out}} as the largest optical telescope in the world.
They are. Everyone is {{looking forward to}} the first images.
